name: Jakob's Law
aliases: Jakob's law of the internet user experience
statement: Users spend most of their time on other sites, so they expect yours to work like the ones they know.
statementAccent: they expect yours to work like the ones they know
meaning: Jakob's Law of the internet user experience states that users spend most of their time on other sites, which means they prefer your site to work the same way as all the other sites they already know. Because people carry expectations built from countless other products and interfaces, designs that follow familiar conventions are easier to use than novel ones. Coined by the usability expert Jakob Nielsen, co-founder of the Nielsen Norman Group, and one of the widely cited Laws of UX, the principle rests on the idea of mental models: users form models of how things work from prior experience, and matching those models lets them focus on their tasks rather than on learning a new interface. It is a foundational principle of interface design about conventions and consistency.
mechanism: People do not approach a new interface fresh; they arrive with mental models assembled from everything else they have used. A shopping-cart icon, a logo in the top-left corner that returns to the home page, a magnifying glass for search, a hamburger menu, all carry meanings learned elsewhere. When a design honours these conventions, it leverages existing mental models and reduces the cognitive load and errors of learning something new, so users can concentrate on their goals. When it violates them, users stumble. The principle also cautions about redesigns: because people dislike having their mental models upended, easing a transition, for instance by letting users temporarily keep an older version, softens the disruption. Familiarity, in short, is usability.

examples.text: A cart icon for checkout, a top-left logo linking home, and a magnifying glass for search all work because users learned them on other sites.
In one study, centring the logo rather than placing it at the left roughly multiplied the number of users who failed to reach the home page in one click, breaking a convention.
When YouTube redesigned in 2017 it let users opt into the old version during the transition, cushioning the violation of their established mental models.

variants.name: Mental models
variants.text: The internal models users build from prior experience of how interfaces work, which a familiar design matches to reduce effort and error.

variants.name: The redesign caveat
variants.text: The guidance that changes to a familiar design should minimise disruption, since users resist having their established expectations overturned.

whyItMatters: Jakob's Law is a cornerstone of user-experience and interface design, capturing why consistency with established conventions is not conservatism but usability. Because users bring expectations from the entire web, designs that respect familiar patterns let people accomplish their goals with minimal learning, while needless novelty imposes a cost that frustrates and drives them away. The principle guides everything from icon choices and navigation layouts to the careful handling of redesigns, and it underlies the broader practice of following platform and design conventions. For designers it is a reminder that the competition sets user expectations, so meeting those expectations is often wiser than reinventing them.

working.text: use familiar patterns, icons, and layouts so users can rely on mental models built from other sites rather than learning yours from scratch.
design so the interface behaves as users already expect, reducing the cognitive load and errors of unfamiliarity.
when redesigning a familiar interface, minimise disruption, for instance by letting users keep the old version for a while, since they resist upended expectations.

limits: Jakob's Law counsels respecting conventions where they exist, but it does not forbid innovation; genuinely better patterns can be worth their learning cost, and slavishly copying competitors can entrench mediocrity. Conventions also vary by platform, culture, and audience, so what is familiar to one group may not be to another. The principle is a design heuristic rather than a hard rule, and it must be balanced against the value of differentiation and improvement. Its evidence is drawn largely from usability practice, so it is a well-supported guideline about expectations, not a precise quantitative law, and knowing when to break a convention is itself a matter of judgement.
misreadings: Jakob's Law does not mean never innovate or blindly copy competitors; it means respect established conventions and user expectations where they exist, because novelty carries a learning cost. It is not an argument against all originality, only against gratuitous unfamiliarity that forces users to relearn basics. And it is a heuristic about expectations, not a guarantee, so it must be weighed against the benefits of a better design and the specifics of the audience, which is why skilled designers sometimes deliberately depart from convention.
origin: Coined by the usability expert Jakob Nielsen, co-founder of the Nielsen Norman Group, and popularised as one of the Laws of UX compiled by Jon Yablonski.

sources.text: Jakob's Law, Laws of UX (Jon Yablonski). — the exact statement, the mental-model and convention implication, and the redesign caveat with the YouTube example.
Jakob's Law of Internet User Experience, Nielsen Norman Group. — Jakob Nielsen's statement that users prefer sites to work like the others they know.
